title: Data Structures and Algorithms
subtitle: Complexity, arrays, lists, hashing, trees, heaps, graphs, sorting, searching, recursion, dynamic programming and greedy methods, with Python labs
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: The core data structures and algorithms every programmer needs, explained intuitively and practised in Python: Big-O, arrays and two pointers, linked lists, stacks and queues, hash tables, trees, heaps, graph traversal, sorting, binary search, recursion and divide and conquer, dynamic programming, and greedy algorithms with shortest paths and spanning trees. Every chapter has an ELI5 block.

chapters.title: Complexity and Big-O
summary: An algorithm is a step-by-step method that solves a problem. We compare algorithms not by seconds on one machine but by how the work grows as the input grows. Big-O notation describes that growth, keeping only the dominant term.

Common classes, from fast to slow, are constant, logarithmic, linear, n log n, quadratic and exponential. Space complexity counts memory in the same way. Amortised analysis averages occasional expensive steps over many cheap ones.
The labs count operations, compare growth rates and find the Big-O class of simple loops.

glossary.def: A finite sequence of precise steps that solves a problem.
An upper bound on growth: f(n) is O(g(n)) if f stays below a constant times g for large n.
How the number of steps grows with input size n.
How the memory used grows with n.
Average cost per operation over a long sequence.
The most work over all inputs of a given size.

keyPoints: Order: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n) < O(n!).
Drop constants and lower terms: 3n^2 + 5n + 2 is O(n^2).
A single loop over n items is O(n); nested loops are O(n^2).
Halving the problem each step gives O(log n).
Appending to a growing array is O(1) amortised.
Big-O is an upper bound; Omega is a lower bound; Theta is both.

items: ELI5. Big-O asks how the work grows when the job gets bigger. Finding a name in a phone book by reading every page grows with the book. Opening to the middle and halving grows very slowly. We care about that growth, not the stopwatch.

How fast is a program? Seconds depend on the machine, so we count steps instead, and ask how the count grows as the input gets bigger. Finding a name in an unsorted list of n names takes up to n looks.
Finding a word in a dictionary takes far fewer, because you can jump to the middle and halve the search each time.

lesson.tex: f(n) = O(g(n)) \iff \exists\, c, n_0:\ f(n) \le c\,g(n)\ \ \forall n \ge n_0

items: Big-O keeps only the part that grows fastest and ignores constant factors. The expression three n squared plus five n plus two is O of n squared, because for big n the square dominates. Doubling n makes an O of n squared algorithm four times slower, but an O of n algorithm only twice as slow.

A few classes cover most programs. Constant time, O of one, does not depend on n, like reading one array cell. Logarithmic time, O of log n, halves the work each step, as in binary search. Linear time scans everything once. N log n is the cost of good sorting. Quadratic time compares all pairs.
Exponential time doubles with each added item and is only usable for tiny inputs.

To analyse code, count the loops. One loop over n items is linear. A loop inside a loop is quadratic. A loop that halves the remaining range is logarithmic. Recursive code gives recurrences, solved later in the divide and conquer chapter.

Sometimes an operation is usually cheap but occasionally costly, like appending to a dynamic array that doubles its storage when full. Amortised analysis spreads the rare cost over all operations and shows the average is constant.
Always state whether you mean the worst, the average or the amortised case.

chapters.title: Arrays, strings and two pointers

maps.title: Arrays
links: String | is | An array of characters
Two pointers | scan | From both ends

summary: An array stores items side by side in memory, so any item is reached by its index in constant time. Inserting or deleting in the middle shifts later items and costs linear time. Dynamic arrays grow by doubling.

Strings are arrays of characters. Many problems on arrays fall to simple patterns: two pointers moving from both ends, a sliding window over a range, and prefix sums that answer range-sum questions in constant time after one pass.
The labs reverse in place, check palindromes, find pairs with a target sum, maximise a window and build prefix sums.

glossary.def: A contiguous block of equal-sized cells indexed from 0.
An array that doubles its capacity when full.
Two indices moving through the data, often from opposite ends.
A range that grows or shrinks as it moves along.
P[i] = sum of the first i items; range sum = P[j] - P[i].
Modifying data without extra storage proportional to n.

keyPoints: Access O(1); search O(n); insert or delete in the middle O(n); append O(1) amortised.
Two pointers on a sorted array finds a pair in O(n).
Sliding window turns an O(n k) scan into O(n).
Prefix sums answer sum(i..j) in O(1) after O(n) setup.
Strings are immutable in many languages: building by repeated joining costs O(n^2).
Check the empty array and one-element cases.

items: ELI5. An array is a row of numbered lockers: you can walk straight to locker 37. Adding a locker in the middle means shifting everyone after it. Two pointers is two people walking toward each other along the row.

Imagine a row of lockers numbered from zero. Because they are side by side, you can walk straight to locker 37 without opening the others. That is an array: any element is available by index in constant time.
The price is that inserting in the middle forces everyone after the new item to shift one place.

A dynamic array hides the fixed size. When full, it allocates a block twice as big and copies the items over. Most appends are cheap and the occasional copy is paid for by the many cheap ones, so appending is constant on average. Python lists work this way.

Two pointers is a favourite trick. To reverse an array, swap the first and last items and move the pointers inward. To find two numbers in a sorted array that add to a target, start at both ends: if the sum is too big, move the right pointer left; if too small, move the left pointer right.
One pass, no nested loops.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} \text{sum}(i..j) = P[j+1] - P[i], \\[0.6em] P[0]=0,\ P[k+1] = P[k] + a_k \end{gathered}

items: A sliding window handles questions about ranges. To find the largest sum of any k consecutive numbers, add the next item and drop the oldest one instead of recomputing the whole range.
Prefix sums do the opposite job: after one pass that stores running totals, the sum of any range is a single subtraction.

Strings are arrays of characters, so the same patterns apply: palindromes by two pointers, longest substring without repeats by a sliding window. A frequent gotcha is that strings can be immutable, so gluing them in a loop copies repeatedly; collect pieces in a list and join once.

practice.title: Reverse in place
practice.intro: Write reverse(a): return the list reversed using two pointers (swap from both ends).
practice.solution:
def reverse(a):
    a = list(a)
    i = 0
    j = len(a) - 1
    while i < j:
        a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
        i += 1
        j -= 1
    return a

chapters.title: Linked lists
summary: A linked list is a chain of nodes; each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. Unlike arrays there is no jump-by-index, but inserting or deleting at a known node needs only pointer changes.

Classic tasks are reversing a list, finding the middle with a fast and a slow pointer, detecting a cycle and merging sorted lists. Doubly linked lists keep a pointer back as well, which makes deletion from both ends easy.
The labs use arrays to simulate nodes: a list of values and a list of next-indices.

glossary.def: A record with a value and a link to another node.
The first node; the entry point to the list.
Each node points only forward.
Each node points forward and backward.
A node whose chain leads back to an earlier node.
Fast pointer moves 2 steps, slow 1; they meet if there is a cycle.

keyPoints: Insert or delete at the head: O(1).
Access or search by position: O(n).
Reverse in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
Fast and slow pointers find the middle and detect cycles.
Linked lists use extra memory for pointers and are cache-unfriendly.
Arrays win for random access; lists win for frequent splicing.

items: ELI5. A linked list is a treasure hunt: each clue says where the next one is. You cannot jump to clue ten, but you can slip a new clue in just by changing two notes. A fast and a slow walker reveal loops, as the fast one laps the slow one.

Picture a treasure hunt where each clue tells you where the next clue is. That is a linked list. Each node stores a value and a reference to the next node, and the head is the first clue. To reach the tenth item you must follow ten links, so access by position costs linear time.

The reward is cheap changes. To insert a new node after a given node, point the new node at that node's successor and the node at the new one: two pointer updates, no shifting. Deleting works the same way. Adding at the head is constant time, which makes linked lists a natural base for stacks.

To reverse a list, walk along it keeping three pointers: the previous node, the current node and the next. At each step, redirect the current node's pointer back to the previous one, then advance. When the walk ends, the previous node is the new head. It takes one pass and no extra storage.

The fast and slow pointer trick finds the middle: move one pointer two steps and another one step, and when the fast one reaches the end the slow one is at the middle. If the list has a cycle, the fast pointer eventually laps the slow one, so they meet. This is Floyd's tortoise and hare algorithm.
A doubly linked list keeps a link backward too, so you can delete a node you are standing on and walk in both directions, at the price of more memory.
In practice arrays are faster for most work because they are laid out contiguously and friendly to the processor cache; linked lists matter when you splice often.

practice.title: Walk a list
practice.intro: A list is given as vals and nxt arrays (nxt[i] is the index of the next node or -1) with head index h. Write to_list(vals, nxt, h): the values in order.

practice.title: Reverse a list
practice.intro: Write reverse_list(vals, nxt, h): reverse the linked list by redirecting pointers (not copying values) and return the values in the new order.
practice.solution:
def reverse_list(vals, nxt, h):
    nxt = list(nxt)
    prev = -1
    cur = h
    while cur != -1:
        n = nxt[cur]
        nxt[cur] = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = n
    out = []
    cur = prev
    while cur != -1:
        out.append(vals[cur])
        cur = nxt[cur]
    return out

practice.title: Middle node
practice.intro: Write middle(vals, nxt, h): the value of the middle node (the second middle for even length), using fast and slow pointers.
practice.solution:
def middle(vals, nxt, h):
    slow = h
    fast = h
    while fast != -1 and nxt[fast] != -1:
        slow = nxt[slow]
        fast = nxt[nxt[fast]]
    return vals[slow]

chapters.title: Stacks, queues and deques

maps.title: Stacks and queues
links: Stack | is | Last in first out
Queue | is | First in first out
Push and pop | change | The top
Enqueue and dequeue | change | The ends

summary: A stack allows adding and removing only at one end: last in, first out, like a pile of plates. A queue adds at the back and removes from the front: first in, first out, like a line at a shop. A deque works at both ends.

Stacks power undo, expression evaluation, bracket matching and the call stack of recursion. Queues power scheduling and breadth-first search. A monotonic stack solves next-greater-element problems in linear time.
The labs match brackets, evaluate postfix expressions, simulate a queue and find the next greater elements.

glossary.def: LIFO structure with push and pop.
FIFO structure with enqueue and dequeue.
Double-ended queue: push and pop at both ends.
The stack of active function calls.
Operators follow operands: 3 4 + means 3 + 4.
A stack kept in sorted order to answer next-greater queries.

keyPoints: All basic stack and queue operations are O(1).
A stack implemented on an array pushes and pops at the end.
A queue on an array uses head and tail indices or a deque.
Balanced brackets: push openers, pop on closers and match.
Postfix evaluation: push numbers, apply operators to the top two.
Next greater element: pop smaller items as larger ones arrive.

items: ELI5. A stack is a pile of plates: last on, first off. A queue is a line at a shop: first in, first served. The undo button is a stack; the print queue is a queue.

A stack is a pile of plates. You add a plate on top and you take a plate from the top, so the last plate in is the first out. The two operations, push and pop, take constant time. Your web browser's back button and your editor's undo are stacks of past states.

Computers use a stack to remember where they were. When a function calls another, the return address goes on the call stack; when the callee finishes, it is popped. Deep recursion can overflow this stack. Any recursive algorithm can be rewritten with an explicit stack.
To check brackets, scan the text. Push each opening bracket; for each closing bracket, pop and check it matches. If the stack is empty at the end and no mismatch occurred, the brackets are balanced.
The same idea evaluates postfix expressions: push numbers, and when an operator arrives, pop two numbers, apply it and push the result.

A queue is the line at a shop: people join at the back and are served from the front. Operating systems queue jobs; breadth-first search uses a queue to explore nearest nodes first. A deque supports both ends and is the standard tool for sliding-window maximum problems.

A monotonic stack keeps its items in sorted order. To find, for each number, the next larger number to its right, scan from left to right and pop every stack item smaller than the new number: the new number is their answer. Each item is pushed and popped once, so the whole scan is linear.

chapters.title: Hash tables

maps.title: Hashing
links: Hash function | maps | Keys to numbers
Collision | is | Two keys one bucket

summary: A hash table stores key-value pairs and finds a key in constant time on average. A hash function turns the key into a number, which picks a bucket. Different keys can land in the same bucket, a collision, handled by chaining or probing.

When the table fills up, the load factor grows and collisions rise, so the table is resized. Python dictionaries and sets are hash tables. They are the first tool for counting, grouping and finding duplicates.
The labs implement a hash function, a chained table, two-sum with a dictionary and frequency counts.

glossary.def: A function mapping a key to an integer bucket index.
Two different keys with the same bucket.
Each bucket holds a list of entries.
On collision, probe other slots in a fixed order.
Number of entries divided by number of buckets.
A hash table that stores keys only.

keyPoints: Average insert, lookup and delete: O(1); worst case O(n).
A good hash spreads keys evenly over buckets.
Resize (double the buckets) when the load factor passes about 0.7.
Keys must be hashable: immutable and with stable hashes.
Use a dictionary for counting, grouping and caching.
Hash tables do not keep sorted order.

items: ELI5. A hash table is a coat check. The ticket number tells the attendant exactly where your coat is, with no searching. Two coats sometimes share a hook, and then they go in a little pile on it.
Suppose you want to find a person's phone number instantly. You could store numbers in an array indexed by a code computed from the name. That code is a hash, and the array is a hash table.
Looking up a key means computing its hash, jumping to that cell and reading the value: constant time, no matter how many entries there are.

A good hash function spreads keys evenly. A simple one for strings multiplies a running total by a prime and adds each character, then takes the remainder by the table size. Since there are far more possible keys than buckets, two keys sometimes collide, by the pigeonhole principle.

There are two main ways to handle collisions. Chaining makes each bucket a small list holding all entries that landed there. Open addressing keeps everything in the array and, on a collision, tries the next slot or another one given by a probe sequence. Both stay fast when the table is not too full.

The load factor is the ratio of entries to buckets. When it grows past a threshold such as seventy percent, the table doubles its bucket array and re-inserts every key. Like the dynamic array, this rare costly step is amortised across many cheap operations.

Hash tables answer the question 'have I seen this before?' in one step, which is why they solve counting words, finding duplicates and the classic two-sum problem: for each number, check whether its complement is already in the dictionary. Their weakness is order: they do not keep keys sorted.

chapters.title: Trees and binary search trees

maps.title: Trees
links: Tree | has | A root and children
Binary tree | has | At most two children
BST | orders | Left smaller right larger

summary: A tree is a hierarchy: a root with children, each a root of its own subtree. A binary tree allows at most two children. A binary search tree keeps smaller keys on the left and larger on the right, so search, insertion and deletion follow one path.

Traversals visit every node: preorder, inorder, postorder and level order. Inorder on a BST gives sorted order. Cost depends on height; balanced trees such as AVL and red-black trees keep the height logarithmic.
The labs build a BST from an array of nodes, search it, compute heights and traverse.

glossary.def: A connected graph with no cycles, rooted at one node.
A binary tree where left < node < right at every node.
The number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path.
A systematic visit of all nodes.
A tree whose height stays O(log n).
A node with no children.

keyPoints: BST search, insert, delete: O(h), with h the height.
Balanced: h = O(log n); degenerate (sorted inserts): h = n.
Inorder (left, node, right) of a BST lists keys sorted.
Preorder copies a tree; postorder deletes it bottom-up.
Level order uses a queue.
AVL and red-black trees rebalance with rotations.

items: ELI5. A binary search tree is a game of higher or lower built into a tree: smaller on the left, bigger on the right. Each step throws away half. If you add things in sorted order the tree becomes a stick and loses its power.

A family tree is a hierarchy: one ancestor at the top, children below, and each child can have children. Computer scientists draw the same shape for file systems, web pages and expressions. The top is the root, nodes without children are leaves, and the height counts the longest path down.

A binary search tree is a tree for fast searching. Every node has a key; everything in its left subtree is smaller, and everything in its right subtree is larger. To find a key, compare it with the node and go left or right, discarding half the tree each time, like binary search.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} \text{search cost} = O(h), \\[0.6em] h \approx \log_2 n \text{ if balanced}, \\[0.6em] h = n \text{ if a chain} \end{gathered}

items: The cost depends on the height. If keys arrive in random order the tree is bushy and the height is about log of n. But inserting sorted keys makes a chain with height n, and search becomes linear.
Self-balancing trees such as AVL and red-black trees fix this by rotating nodes after inserts and deletes, guaranteeing logarithmic height.

Traversals visit each node exactly once. Inorder goes left, node, right and prints a BST in sorted order. Preorder visits the node first and is used to copy a tree. Postorder visits children first and is used to delete one or evaluate an expression tree. Level order uses a queue and goes row by row.

Deleting from a BST has three cases. A leaf is removed outright. A node with one child is replaced by that child. A node with two children is replaced by its inorder successor, the smallest key in the right subtree, which keeps the ordering intact.

practice.title: BST search
practice.intro: A BST is given as arrays key, left, right (child index or -1) with root 0. Write bst_has(key, left, right, t): 1 if t is in the tree else 0.

practice.title: Inorder traversal
practice.intro: Write inorder(key, left, right): the keys by inorder traversal from root 0.
practice.solution:
def inorder(key, left, right):
    out = []
    st = []
    cur = 0
    while cur != -1 or st:
        while cur != -1:
            st.append(cur)
            cur = left[cur]
        cur = st.pop()
        out.append(key[cur])
        cur = right[cur]
    return out

practice.title: Tree height
practice.intro: Write height(left, right): the height (edges on the longest root-to-leaf path) of the tree rooted at 0; a single node has height 0.

practice.title: Build a BST by insertion
practice.intro: Write build_inorder(keys): insert the distinct keys one by one into a BST (as nodes in arrays) and return the inorder keys, which must come out sorted.
practice.solution:
def build_inorder(keys):
    key = []
    left = []
    right = []
    for k in keys:
        key.append(k)
        left.append(-1)
        right.append(-1)
        i = len(key) - 1
        if i == 0:
            continue
        cur = 0
        while True:
            if k < key[cur]:
                if left[cur] == -1:
                    left[cur] = i
                    break
                cur = left[cur]
            else:
                if right[cur] == -1:
                    right[cur] = i
                    break
                cur = right[cur]
    out = []
    st = []
    cur = 0 if key else -1
    while cur != -1 or st:
        while cur != -1:
            st.append(cur)
            cur = left[cur]
        cur = st.pop()
        out.append(key[cur])
        cur = right[cur]
    return out

chapters.title: Heaps and priority queues

maps.title: Heaps
links: Priority queue | serves | The best item first
Binary heap | is | A complete tree in an array
Heap sort | sorts | In O(n log n)

summary: A priority queue always serves the item with the highest priority next, like an emergency room. A binary heap implements it as a complete binary tree stored in an array where each parent is no larger than its children (a min-heap).

Push adds at the end and sifts up; pop removes the top, moves the last item to the root and sifts down. Both take logarithmic time. Heapify builds a heap from n items in linear time, and heap sort uses it. Heaps power Dijkstra's algorithm and top-k queries.
The labs implement push and pop, heapify, heap sort and a top-k selector.

glossary.def: An abstract type with insert and extract-min (or max).
A complete binary tree with the heap property, stored in an array.
In a min-heap each parent is at most its children.
Swap an item with its parent or smaller child to restore order.
Turn an arbitrary array into a heap in O(n).
Keep a heap of size k to find the k largest items.

keyPoints: Array layout: parent of i is (i-1)//2; children are 2i+1 and 2i+2.
Push and pop are O(log n); peek is O(1).
Heapify is O(n); heap sort is O(n log n) and in place.
A min-heap gives the smallest quickly, not full sorted order.
Top-k of n items: O(n log k) with a size-k heap.
Dijkstra and Huffman coding use heaps.

items: ELI5. A heap is a tournament bracket where the winner is always on top. Take the winner out, let the last player take the seat, and let them sink down until the bracket is fair again. You always get the best next.

In a hospital, the sickest patient is treated first, not the one who arrived first. A priority queue behaves like this: you may insert anything at any time, and the next item out is always the most urgent. A sorted list would do, but inserting into it costs linear time.
A heap does both operations in logarithmic time.

A binary heap is a complete binary tree: every level is full except possibly the last, which fills from the left. That shape fits perfectly in an array. The root is at index zero. The children of node i sit at 2i plus 1 and 2i plus 2, and its parent at i minus 1 divided by two, rounded down.
In a min-heap each parent is no larger than its children, so the smallest item is always at the root. To push, put the new item at the end and swap it with its parent while it is smaller.
To pop, take the root, move the last item to the root and swap it downward with its smaller child until the order is restored. Each walk is at most the height, log n.
Building a heap from a whole array can be done in linear time: starting from the last parent, sift each node down. Heap sort builds a max-heap and repeatedly swaps the top into the sorted tail.
Heaps also answer top-k questions: keep a small heap of the k best so far and replace its smallest when something better arrives.

practice.intro: Write pop(h): return [smallest, rest-of-heap-list] after removing the root (sift down). h is non-empty.
practice.solution:
def pop(h):
    h = list(h)
    top = h[0]
    last = h.pop()
    if h:
        h[0] = last
        i = 0
        n = len(h)
        while True:
            l = 2 * i + 1
            r = 2 * i + 2
            s = i
            if l < n and h[l] < h[s]:
                s = l
            if r < n and h[r] < h[s]:
                s = r
            if s == i:
                break
            h[i], h[s] = h[s], h[i]
            i = s
    return [top, h]

chapters.title: Graphs and traversal
summary: Graphs model networks of things and links. Stored as adjacency lists, they use memory proportional to vertices plus edges. Two traversals underlie almost every graph algorithm: breadth-first search with a queue and depth-first search with a stack or recursion.
A visited set keeps traversals from looping. BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs, DFS finds connected components, detects cycles and gives topological orders of dependency graphs.
The labs build adjacency lists, run BFS and DFS, count components and sort tasks topologically.

glossary.def: For each vertex, the list of its neighbours.
Visit nearest vertices first, using a queue.
Follow a path as deep as possible, then backtrack.
A maximal set of mutually reachable vertices.
A directed graph with no cycles.
Vertices ordered so each edge goes forward.

keyPoints: BFS and DFS both run in O(V + E).
BFS gives fewest-edge paths in unweighted graphs.
DFS timestamps help find cycles and components.
Adjacency lists suit sparse graphs; matrices suit dense ones.
Topological order exists only for DAGs.
Always mark a vertex visited when you first reach it.

items: ELI5. Breadth-first search is a ripple on a pond, moving out ring by ring. Depth-first search is exploring a cave, going as deep as you can, then backing up. Both mark where they have been so they never go round in circles.

A graph is a set of vertices joined by edges. Maps, social networks, the web and course prerequisites are graphs. To store one, give each vertex a list of its neighbours. That takes memory proportional to the number of vertices plus edges, much better than an n by n table when few links exist.

Breadth-first search starts at a source and visits all neighbours, then their neighbours, and so on, using a queue. Because it explores in rings, the first time it reaches a vertex is along a path with the fewest edges. It runs in time proportional to vertices plus edges.

Depth-first search goes the other way: follow one path as far as it goes, then back up and try the next branch. It uses a stack, or recursion, which is the same thing. Marking vertices as visited stops it from going round cycles forever.
It is the basis for finding connected components, checking for cycles and finding strongly connected components.

A topological sort orders the tasks of a dependency graph so every task comes after the tasks it needs. A simple method repeatedly removes a vertex with no incoming edges, Kahn's algorithm. If some vertices are left over, the graph has a cycle and no order exists.
Build tools and course planners use it all the time.

practice.intro: Write bfs(n, edges, s): the vertices in BFS visiting order from s (neighbours in ascending order).
practice.hint: A queue and a seen list.
practice.solution:
def bfs(n, edges, s):
    a = [[] for i in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        a[u].append(v)
        a[v].append(u)
    a = [sorted(x) for x in a]
    seen = [0] * n
    seen[s] = 1
    q = [s]
    i = 0
    while i < len(q):
        x = q[i]
        i += 1
        for y in a[x]:
            if not seen[y]:
                seen[y] = 1
                q.append(y)
    return q

practice.title: Topological sort
practice.intro: Write topo(n, edges): a topological order of a DAG of directed edges [u, v] using Kahn's algorithm; always take the smallest available vertex. Return [] if there is a cycle.
practice.solution:
def topo(n, edges):
    indeg = [0] * n
    out = [[] for i in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        out[u].append(v)
        indeg[v] += 1
    ready = [i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0]
    res = []
    while ready:
        ready.sort()
        x = ready.pop(0)
        res.append(x)
        for y in out[x]:
            indeg[y] -= 1
            if indeg[y] == 0:
                ready.append(y)
    return res if len(res) == n else []

chapters.title: Sorting

maps.title: Sorting
links: Insertion | inserts | Into a sorted prefix
Quick sort | partitions | Around a pivot

summary: Sorting puts items in order and makes many other tasks easier, such as searching and finding duplicates. Simple methods like bubble and insertion sort take quadratic time. Merge sort and quick sort take n log n.

Merge sort splits, sorts each half and merges, and it is stable. Quick sort partitions around a pivot and is fast on average. Comparison sorting cannot beat n log n, but counting sort uses the key values to reach linear time for small integer keys.
The labs implement insertion sort, merge, quick sort partition and counting sort.

glossary.def: Keeps the original order of equal items.
Uses O(1) extra memory.
Divide, sort halves, merge: O(n log n) always.
Partition around a pivot: O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst.
Counts each key; O(n + k) for keys in 0..k.
Any comparison sort needs Omega(n log n) comparisons.

keyPoints: Insertion sort: O(n^2) worst, O(n) on nearly sorted data.
Merge sort: O(n log n), O(n) extra space, stable.
Quick sort: O(n log n) average, in place, not stable.
Heap sort: O(n log n), in place.
Counting and radix sort: linear for bounded keys.
Library sorts (Timsort) combine merge and insertion sort.

items: ELI5. Sorting is arranging cards. Insertion sort slides each card into place. Merge sort splits the pile, sorts each half and zips them together. Quick sort picks a card and puts smaller ones left and bigger ones right.

Sorting is like arranging a hand of playing cards. Insertion sort does what you do naturally: take the next card and slide it into its place among the cards already sorted. For n cards it may take up to n squared moves, but if the hand is almost sorted it is very fast.

Merge sort splits the array in half, sorts each half recursively and merges the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front item. There are log n levels of splitting, each costing n for the merges, so the total is n log n, whatever the input.
It needs extra memory for merging but is stable.
Quick sort picks a pivot, moves smaller items to its left and larger to its right, and recurses on both sides. On average it takes n log n and works in place, which makes it very fast in practice.
A bad pivot, such as the smallest item every time, degrades it to n squared, so pivots are chosen randomly or by median of three.

There is a limit: any sorting method that works only by comparing items needs at least about n log n comparisons, because it must distinguish among n factorial orderings. To go faster you must use more than comparisons.
Counting sort tallies how many times each small integer occurs and writes them out in order, in time linear in n plus the key range.

A sort is stable if equal items keep their relative order, which matters when sorting records by one field after another. The sort in your language library is usually Timsort, a stable hybrid of merge and insertion sort that exploits runs already in order.

practice.intro: Write merge(a, b): merge two sorted lists into one sorted list.
practice.solution:
def merge(a, b):
    i = 0
    j = 0
    out = []
    while i < len(a) and j < len(b):
        if a[i] <= b[j]:
            out.append(a[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            out.append(b[j])
            j += 1
    out.extend(a[i:])
    out.extend(b[j:])
    return out

chapters.title: Searching and binary search

maps.title: Searching
links: Binary search | halves | A sorted range
Search on answer | binary searches | A property

summary: Linear search checks every item, taking linear time. If the data is sorted, binary search compares with the middle item and discards half the range each step, taking logarithmic time.

Binary search is easy to describe and easy to get wrong. A clear invariant, the answer lies within the current range, prevents off-by-one errors. Variants find the first or last position of a value. You can also binary search over an answer, such as the smallest speed that finishes in time.
The labs write binary search, find insertion points, count occurrences and search on an answer.

glossary.def: Repeatedly halve a sorted range by comparing with the middle.
A condition true at each loop step that proves correctness.
The first index whose item is not less than the target.
A yes/no test that is false then true as the input grows.
Using lo or hi one place wrong.
Guess the position from the value, for uniform data.

keyPoints: Binary search needs sorted data and random access.
Time O(log n): 1000 items need at most 10 steps; a billion need 30.
Use mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2 in languages with fixed-width integers.
Decide the invariant first, then write the loop.
Lower bound gives insertion points and counts via two searches.
Search on answer works whenever a yes/no test is monotonic.

items: ELI5. Binary search is guessing a number by asking higher or lower. Each guess halves the choices, so a thousand needs ten guesses. The trick is to keep a promise: the answer is always inside my current range.

Guess a number between one and a thousand. If I only say higher or lower, you can always find it in ten guesses: ask about 500, then 250 or 750, and so on. Each guess halves what remains. This is binary search, and it works on any sorted array.

The idea is simple, but small mistakes are common: infinite loops, skipping the answer, reading outside the array. The cure is to state an invariant. For example: the target, if present, lies in positions lo to hi inclusive. Each step must keep that true while shrinking the range.

A useful variant is the lower bound: the first position whose item is at least the target. It gives the insertion point for a new item in a sorted list. The number of occurrences of a value is the upper bound minus the lower bound, two searches.
Binary search is not only for arrays. Whenever a yes/no question is monotonic, false for small inputs and true from some point on, you can binary search for the switch.

What is the smallest speed that lets a machine finish a job in eight hours? Test a speed; if it works, try slower, otherwise faster. This search on the answer solves many problems that look hard at first.

chapters.title: Recursion and divide and conquer

maps.title: Recursion
links: Divide and conquer | splits | Then combines

summary: Recursion solves a problem by solving smaller versions of the same problem. Every recursive function needs a base case that stops it and a step that makes progress toward it. The call stack remembers pending work.

Divide and conquer splits a problem into parts, solves them recursively and combines the answers. Merge sort and binary search are examples. The cost is written as a recurrence, and the master theorem gives its solution.
Backtracking explores choices and undoes them to enumerate subsets, permutations and puzzles.
The labs write recursive functions, count recurrence cost and enumerate subsets and permutations.

glossary.def: The smallest input answered directly.
Reduces the problem and calls the function again.
Split, solve parts, combine.
A formula giving the cost in terms of smaller inputs.
Build a solution step by step, undoing choices that fail.
A recursive call as the very last action.

keyPoints: Always write the base case first.
T(n) = a T(n/b) + O(n^d): compare a with b^d (master theorem).
Binary search: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) = O(log n).
Merge sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n).
Naive Fibonacci is exponential; caching makes it linear.
Subsets: 2^n; permutations: n!.

items: ELI5. Recursion is Russian dolls: open one and find a smaller set inside, until the last doll that does not open. Divide and conquer splits a job into halves, does each half, and joins the answers.

Russian dolls: to open the whole set, open the biggest doll and find a smaller set of dolls inside. Keep going until the last tiny doll that does not open. Recursion works this way. A function solves a big problem by calling itself on a smaller one.
The tiny doll is the base case, and without it the calls never stop.

A classic example is the factorial. By definition, n factorial is n times the factorial of n minus one, and the factorial of zero is one. The function calls itself with a smaller number each time until it reaches zero, then the pending multiplications finish on the way back.
The computer remembers them on the call stack.

Divide and conquer is recursion with three steps: divide the problem into parts, conquer each part recursively and combine the answers. Merge sort divides the array in half, sorts each half and merges. Fast exponentiation computes a to the n by squaring a to the n over two.
Many geometric and numeric algorithms follow this pattern.

lesson.tex: T(n) = a\,T(n/b) + O(n^d) \;\Rightarrow\; T(n)=\begin{cases}O(n^d) & a<b^d\\ O(n^d\log n) & a=b^d\\ O(n^{\log_b a}) & a>b^d\end{cases}

items: The master theorem reads the cost off the recurrence. Merge sort has a equal to two, b equal to two and d equal to one: a equals b to the d, so the answer is n log n. Binary search has a equal to one, b equal to two and d equal to zero, again balanced, giving log n.
Backtracking explores choices one at a time. To list all subsets, for each item either include it or not, recurse, then undo the choice. The tree of choices has two to the n leaves.
It is also how puzzle solvers like sudoku and the n-queens problem work, cutting off branches that already break the rules.

practice.intro: Write subsets(a): the list of all subsets of a, each a list in input order, ordered by backtracking where each item is first excluded then included. For [1,2] the result is [[], [2], [1], [1, 2]].
practice.solution:
def subsets(a):
    out = []
    cur = []
    def go(i):
        if i == len(a):
            out.append(list(cur))
            return
        go(i + 1)
        cur.append(a[i])
        go(i + 1)
        cur.pop()
    go(0)
    return out

practice.hint: Pick each unused item in turn.
practice.solution:
def perms(a):
    out = []
    used = [0] * len(a)
    cur = []
    def go():
        if len(cur) == len(a):
            out.append(list(cur))
            return
        for i in range(len(a)):
            if not used[i]:
                used[i] = 1
                cur.append(a[i])
                go()
                cur.pop()
                used[i] = 0
    go()
    return out

chapters.title: Dynamic programming

maps.title: Dynamic programming
links: Knapsack | picks | Items under a limit

summary: Dynamic programming solves problems whose recursive solution repeats the same subproblems. By storing each answer once, either top-down with a cache or bottom-up with a table, exponential work becomes polynomial.

The recipe is to define the state, write the transition that builds a state from smaller ones, set the base cases and read off the answer. Classic problems include Fibonacci, coin change, the knapsack, the longest common subsequence and edit distance.
The labs solve Fibonacci, coin change, 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence and edit distance.

glossary.def: The same smaller problem is needed many times.
An optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems.
Top-down recursion with a cache.
Bottom-up filling of a table.
The parameters that identify a subproblem.
The rule computing a state from smaller states.

keyPoints: Cost is (number of states) x (cost per transition).
Fibonacci: F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2); O(n) with a cache.
Coin change: ways[a] sums ways[a - coin] over coins.
Knapsack: best[i][w] = max(skip item, take item).
LCS: match extends the diagonal; else take the max of two neighbours.
Space can often be reduced to one or two rows.

items: ELI5. Dynamic programming is writing down answers so you never solve the same puzzle twice. Like a student keeping a notebook of solved sums: before working one out, check the notebook.

The naive recursive Fibonacci recomputes the same values again and again: computing F of fifty makes billions of calls. The fix is to remember. Each time you compute a value, store it; next time just look it up. This simple idea, remember what you computed, is dynamic programming.

There are two styles. In memoisation you keep the recursive code and add a dictionary: before computing, check the cache. In tabulation you fill a table from the smallest subproblems upward, so no recursion is needed. Both give the same result and the same running time; tabulation uses less stack.

Designing a solution follows a recipe. First choose the state: what numbers describe a subproblem? Then find the transition: how is the answer for a state built from answers of smaller ones? Then set the base cases, decide the order to fill the table and say where the final answer sits.
The cost is the number of states times the work per state.

In the 0/1 knapsack you may take or leave each item to maximise value under a weight limit. For each item and each capacity, either skip the item, or take it and use the remaining capacity best from before. The table has items times capacity cells, so it runs in pseudo-polynomial time.

Sequence problems use two-dimensional tables. The longest common subsequence of two strings extends the diagonal when the characters match, and otherwise takes the better of dropping a character from either string.
Edit distance, the fewest insertions, deletions and replacements to turn one word into another, is similar and powers spell checkers.

chapters.title: Greedy algorithms, shortest paths and spanning trees

maps.title: Greedy
links: Minimum spanning tree | connects | At least cost

summary: A greedy algorithm makes the best-looking choice at each step and never looks back. It is fast and simple, and for the right problems it is provably optimal. The proof usually shows that an optimal solution can be changed to include the greedy choice.

Classic greedy results: choosing the most intervals by earliest finish time, Huffman coding, Dijkstra's shortest paths with non-negative weights, and Kruskal's and Prim's minimum spanning trees. Union-find is the data structure that makes Kruskal fast.
The labs schedule intervals, run Dijkstra, build a minimum spanning tree with union-find and compute Huffman code cost.

glossary.def: Take the locally best option and commit.
Show swapping into the greedy choice never hurts.
Repeatedly settle the unsettled vertex with the smallest distance.
A tree that connects all vertices.
Structure with find (which set) and union (merge sets).
A prefix code with shorter codes for frequent symbols.

keyPoints: Interval scheduling: sort by finish time, take every compatible interval.
Dijkstra with a heap: O((V + E) log V); needs non-negative weights.
Kruskal: sort edges, add if they join different components; O(E log E).
Prim: grow a tree from a vertex by the cheapest edge out.
Union-find with path compression is almost O(1) per operation.
Greedy fails for coin change with odd coin sets and for knapsack.

items: ELI5. A greedy algorithm always takes the best-looking choice right now, like picking the closest next shop. It is quick, and for the right problems it is perfect, but sometimes the nearest choice leads you astray.

A greedy algorithm is like making change: give the biggest coin that fits, then repeat. For ordinary currencies this gives the fewest coins, but with coins of one, three and four, making six by greed takes four, one and one when two threes would do.
Greedy is only right for problems with the right structure, and each use needs a proof.
Interval scheduling asks to fit the most non-overlapping meetings in one room. The best greedy rule is surprising: always pick the meeting that finishes earliest.
The proof is an exchange argument: in any optimal schedule you can swap the first meeting for the earliest-finishing one without losing any.

Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from a source in a graph with non-negative edge weights. Keep a tentative distance for every vertex. Repeatedly take the unsettled vertex with the smallest distance, settle it, and relax its edges: if going through it makes a neighbour closer, update.
A heap makes the choice fast.

A minimum spanning tree connects all vertices with the least total edge weight. Kruskal's algorithm sorts the edges and adds each one unless it would form a cycle. To test for a cycle quickly we use union-find: each component is a set; find returns its representative and union merges two sets.

Huffman coding builds the best prefix code for compression. Repeatedly take the two least frequent symbols and join them under a new node whose weight is the sum. Frequent symbols end up near the top with short codes. The total cost is the sum of all the merged weights.

practice.title: Huffman cost
practice.intro: Write huffman(freqs): the total weighted cost of the Huffman code: repeatedly merge the two smallest frequencies, adding their sum to the cost.
practice.solution:
def huffman(freqs):
    h = sorted(freqs)
    cost = 0
    while len(h) > 1:
        a = h.pop(0)
        b = h.pop(0)
        cost += a + b
        h.append(a + b)
        h.sort()
    return cost
